content: Kleine-Levin syndrome (KLS) is a rare neurological disorder that predominantly affects adolescent males. It is characterized by recurrent episodes of excessive sleepiness (hypersomnia), which are often accompanied by excessive eating (hyperphagia), cognitive impairments, mood disturbances, abnormal behaviors such as hypersexuality, and symptoms of autonomic dysfunction. In 1990, the diagnostic criteria for KLS were revised in the International Classification of Sleep Disorders, defining it as a condition involving recurring episodes of extreme sleepiness lasting several days, which may or may not be associated with hyperphagia and abnormal behaviors. In the 2014 revision of the International Classification of Sleep Disorders (ICSD-3), KLS was further defined as a disorder marked by recurrent episodes of hypersomnia lasting between two days and four weeks, with episodes recurring at least annually. These episodes are typically accompanied by hyperphagia, and the condition most commonly begins in early adolescence in males, though it can occasionally present later in life or in females. A monosymptomatic form of KLS, characterized solely by hypersomnia without binge eating or hypersexuality, can also occur. The underlying cause of KLS remains unknown. Various treatment strategies have been attempted, and some medications have shown potential benefits in managing the condition. However, due to the rarity of KLS, there is a lack of long-term follow-up studies or established therapeutic protocols. The objective of this review was to assess whether pharmacological treatments for KLS are effective and safe, and to determine which specific drugs or drug categories might be beneficial. To achieve this, a comprehensive search was conducted across multiple databases, including the Cochrane Epilepsy Group Specialized Register, CENTRAL, MEDLINE, LILACS, ClinicalTrials.gov, and the WHO International Clinical Trials Registry Platform, as well as reference lists from sleep medicine textbooks and review articles. The search was last updated on April 7, 2016. The review aimed to include all randomized controlled trials (RCTs) and quasi-randomized controlled trials that investigated pharmacological interventions for KLS. Both parallel-group and cross-over study designs were considered eligible. Two authors were prepared to extract data from the identified studies. However, no studies met the inclusion criteria for this systematic review. As a result, the authors concluded that there is a critical need for therapeutic trials of pharmacological treatments for KLS using a double-blind, placebo-controlled design to establish evidence-based management strategies for this condition.
